claim: RAI1 haploinsufficiency causes Smith–Magenis syndrome (SMS), a genetic disorder with symptoms including hyperphagia, hyperlipidemia, severe obesity, and autism phenotypes.
source: Retinoic acid-induced 1 (RAI1) haploinsufficiency causes Smith–Magenis syndrome (SMS), a genetic disorder with symptoms including hyperphagia, hyperlipidemia, severe obesity, and autism phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about SMS and RAI1.

claim: RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator with a pan-neural expression pattern and hundreds of downstream targets.
source: RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator with a pan-neural expression pattern and hundreds of downstream targets.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about RAI1.

claim: Hypothalamic brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its downstream signalling are disrupted in SMS (Rai1+/-) mice.
source: Here we find that hypothalamic brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its downstream signalling are disrupted in SMS (Rai1+/-) mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Selective Rai1 loss from all BDNF-producing cells induced obesity in mice.
source: Selective Rai1 loss from all BDNF-producing cells or from BDNF-producing neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) induced obesity in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Selective Rai1 loss from BDNF-producing neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) induced obesity in mice.
source: Selective Rai1 loss from all BDNF-producing cells or from BDNF-producing neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) induced obesity in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Rai1 ablation decreased the intrinsic excitability of PVHBDNF neurons.
source: Electrophysiological recordings revealed that Rai1 ablation decreased the intrinsic excitability of PVHBDNF neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3.

claim: Chronic treatment of SMS mice with LM22A-4 engages neurotrophin downstream signalling and delayed obesity onset.
source: Chronic treatment of SMS mice with LM22A-4 engages neurotrophin downstream signalling and delayed obesity onset.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued disrupted lipid profiles in SMS mice.
source: This treatment also partially rescued disrupted lipid profiles, insulin intolerance, and stereotypical repetitive behaviour in SMS mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued insulin intolerance in SMS mice.
source: This treatment also partially rescued disrupted lipid profiles, insulin intolerance, and stereotypical repetitive behaviour in SMS mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued stereotypical repetitive behaviour in SMS mice.
source: This treatment also partially rescued disrupted lipid profiles, insulin intolerance, and stereotypical repetitive behaviour in SMS mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: 20% of the world's adult population is expected to become obese by 2025 if current trends persist.
source: Obesity is an increasing global concern: 20% of the world's adult population is expected to become obese by 2025 if current trends persist (Collaboration NCDRF, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from an external source (Collaboration NCDRF, 2017).

claim: Eighty percent of SMS cases are caused by interstitial deletions of the 17p11.2 chromosomal region containing a dosage-sensitive gene, retinoic acid-induced 1 (RAI1).
source: Eighty percent of SMS cases are caused by interstitial deletions of the 17p11.2 chromosomal region containing a dosage-sensitive gene, retinoic acid-induced 1 (RAI1) (Slager et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from an external source (Slager et al., 2003).

claim: 40% of SMS patients are above the 95th percentile weight.
source: Most SMS patients are overweight (40% >95th percentile weight, 80% >85th percentile weight) and exhibit overeating tendencies by adolescence (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).

claim: 80% of SMS patients are above the 85th percentile weight.
source: Most SMS patients are overweight (40% >95th percentile weight, 80% >85th percentile weight) and exhibit overeating tendencies by adolescence (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).

claim: SMS patients exhibit overeating tendencies by adolescence.
source: Most SMS patients are overweight (40% >95th percentile weight, 80% >85th percentile weight) and exhibit overeating tendencies by adolescence (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Alaimo et al., 2015; Burns et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2022).

claim: Twenty percent of SMS patients do not have 17p11.2 deletions but instead carry RAI1 point mutations that are still frequently associated with obesity.
source: Twenty percent of SMS patients do not have 17p11.2 deletions but instead carry RAI1 point mutations that are still frequently associated with obesity (Boot et al., 2021; Edelman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Boot et al., 2021; Edelman et al., 2007).

claim: The human RAI1 protein shares >80% sequence identity with the mouse RAI1 protein.
source: The human RAI1 protein shares >80% sequence identity with the mouse RAI1 protein, allowing us to study RAI1 function in vivo (Huang et al., 2016; Javed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Huang et al., 2016; Javed et al., 2020).

claim: Rai1 encodes a transcriptional regulator that binds to the promoter or enhancer regions of its target genes, most of which are involved in neurodevelopment and synaptic transmission.
source: We previously found that Rai1 encodes a transcriptional regulator that binds to the promoter or enhancer regions of its target genes, most of which are involved in neurodevelopment and synaptic transmission (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Huang et al., 2016).

claim: SMS (Rai1+/-) mice exhibit obesity associated with hyperphagia and increased adiposity.
source: SMS (Rai1+/-) mice exhibit obesity associated with hyperphagia and increased adiposity (Burns et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Burns et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2016).

claim: Female SMS mice exhibit more pronounced obesity than males.
source: Interestingly, RAI1 may have a sexually dimorphic function as female SMS mice exhibit more pronounced obesity than males (Burns et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Burns et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2016).

claim: Rai1 deletion in either subcortical excitatory neurons (vGlut2+) or single-minded homolog 1 (Sim1+) neurons induced obesity in mice.
source: Using a homozygous Rai1 conditional knockout (Rai1-cKO) mice, we found that Rai1 deletion in either subcortical excitatory neurons (vGlut2+) or single-minded homolog 1 (Sim1+) neurons induced obesity in mice (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Huang et al., 2016).

claim: Deleting Bdnf from the PVH results in obesity due to increased food intake, reduced energy expenditure, and reduced locomotion.
source: Deleting Bdnf from the PVH results in obesity due to increased food intake, reduced energy expenditure, and reduced locomotion (An et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from an external source (An et al., 2015).

claim: Activation of PVHBDNF neurons results in weight loss.
source: While PVH neuronal activity is reduced during feeding (Xu et al., 2019), activation of PVHBDNF neurons results in weight loss (Wu and Xu, 2022).
evidence: This is cited from an external source (Wu and Xu, 2022).

claim: RAI1 promotes Bdnf expression in the hypothalamus throughout life.
source: We recently found that RAI1 promotes Bdnf expression in the hypothalamus throughout life (Javed et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Javed et al., 2021).

claim: Patients carrying monogenic mutations in either BDNF or NTRK2 (encoding TRKB) experience severe hyperphagic obesity.
source: Patients carrying monogenic mutations in either BDNF (Gray et al., 2006) or NTRK2 (encoding TRKB) (Yeo et al., 2004) experience severe hyperphagic obesity.
evidence: This is cited from external sources (Gray et al., 2006; Yeo et al., 2004).

claim: Obesity and associated metabolic dysfunctions such as impaired glucose and insulin sensitivity are correlated with impaired PI3K-AKT pathway.
source: Moreover, obesity and associated metabolic dysfunctions such as impaired glucose and insulin sensitivity are correlated with impaired PI3K-AKT pathway, a TRKB downstream target (Su et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from an external source (Su et al., 2021).

claim: Bdnf overexpression during early embryonic development protected SMS (Rai1+/-) mice from weight gain and metabolic defects.
source: Given that (1) Bdnf overexpression during early embryonic development or (2) targeting Bdnf overexpression to the PVH of adolescent SMS (Rai1+/-) mice protected them from weight gain and metabolic defects (Javed et al., 2021), and that (3) a point mutation in RAI1 disrupts its ability to transcriptionally enhance BDNF expression in vitro (Abad et al., 2018), pharmacological targeting of neurotrophin downstream signalling is an attractive and yet unexplored therapeutic avenue for SMS.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Javed et al., 2021).

claim: Targeting Bdnf overexpression to the PVH of adolescent SMS (Rai1+/-) mice protected them from weight gain and metabolic defects.
source: Given that (1) Bdnf overexpression during early embryonic development or (2) targeting Bdnf overexpression to the PVH of adolescent SMS (Rai1+/-) mice protected them from weight gain and metabolic defects (Javed et al., 2021), and that (3) a point mutation in RAI1 disrupts its ability to transcriptionally enhance BDNF expression in vitro (Abad et al., 2018), pharmacological targeting of neurotrophin downstream signalling is an attractive and yet unexplored therapeutic avenue for SMS.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Javed et al., 2021).

claim: A point mutation in RAI1 disrupts its ability to transcriptionally enhance BDNF expression in vitro.
source: Given that (1) Bdnf overexpression during early embryonic development or (2) targeting Bdnf overexpression to the PVH of adolescent SMS (Rai1+/-) mice protected them from weight gain and metabolic defects (Javed et al., 2021), and that (3) a point mutation in RAI1 disrupts its ability to transcriptionally enhance BDNF expression in vitro (Abad et al., 2018), pharmacological targeting of neurotrophin downstream signalling is an attractive and yet unexplored therapeutic avenue for SMS.
evidence: This is cited from an external source (Abad et al., 2018).

claim: BDNF protein levels were significantly reduced in 7-week-old pre-symptomatic SMS mice relative to controls.
source: To determine if BDNF protein levels were consequently altered in the hypothalamus, we performed an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and found that BDNF protein levels were significantly reduced in 7-week-old pre-symptomatic SMS mice relative to controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Control and SMS samples are clustered separately in the principal component analysis.
source: Control and SMS samples are clustered separately in the principal component analysis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA plot shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most differentially expressed phosphorylated proteins were downregulated in SMS mice.
source: Hierarchical clustering analysis indicated that most differentially expressed phosphorylated proteins (Figure 1D) and total proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were downregulated in SMS mice.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most differentially expressed total proteins were downregulated in SMS mice.
source: Hierarchical clustering analysis indicated that most differentially expressed phosphorylated proteins (Figure 1D) and total proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were downregulated in SMS mice.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of connected nodes downregulated in SMS (FDR < 10e-5) belong to the neurotrophin, PI3K-AKT, and mTOR signalling cascades.
source: We mapped total proteins, as well as phospho-proteins, that were differentially expressed in Ctrl and SMS samples onto the interconnected biological network and identified a subset of connected nodes downregulated in SMS (FDR < 10e-5) belong to the neurotrophin, PI3K-AKT, and mTOR signalling cascades (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by protein-protein interaction analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The expression levels of PIK3CA were significantly reduced in the SMS mice compared to controls.
source: The expression levels of PIK3CA, a common node in these pathways, were significantly reduced in the SMS mice compared to controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression levels of phosphorylated NF-κB were significantly reduced in the SMS group.
source: Moreover, the expression levels of phosphorylated NF-κB (nuclear factor-kappa B), a downstream target of the neurotrophin pathway, were significantly reduced in the SMS group (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ai9 signals faithfully reflected endogenous BDNF protein expression in the PVH.
source: We crossed the BdnfCre/+ mice with tdTomato-Ai9 reporter mice and found that Ai9 signals faithfully reflected endogenous BDNF protein expression in the PVH (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: 55% of PVHBDNF neurons express RAI1.
source: Specifically, 55% of PVHBDNF neurons express RAI1, whereas only 2% of PVHOxytocin neurons express RAI1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Only 2% of PVHOxytocin neurons express RAI1.
source: Specifically, 55% of PVHBDNF neurons express RAI1, whereas only 2% of PVHOxytocin neurons express RAI1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Conditional knockout mice (cKO: BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/fl) showed a significant reduction in Rai1 expression in PVHBDNF neurons compared to controls.
source: Conditional knockout mice (cKO: BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/fl) showed a significant reduction in Rai1 expression in PVHBDNF neurons compared to controls (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The total number of BDNF-producing cells in the PVH remained similar in Ctrl and cKO mice.
source: The total number of BDNF-producing cells in the PVH remained similar in Ctrl and cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), indicating that RAI1 loss did not affect PVH neurogenesis or survival.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Female cKO mice showed a significant weight gain when compared to female Ctrl mice.
source: We monitored body weight weekly and found that male and female cKO mice showed a significant increase in body weight beginning at 15 wk of age compared to controls (Ctrl: BdnfCre/+) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Male cKO mice showed a significant increase in body weight beginning at 15 wk of age compared to controls.
source: We monitored body weight weekly and found that male and female cKO mice showed a significant increase in body weight beginning at 15 wk of age compared to controls (Ctrl: BdnfCre/+) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Conditional Rai1 heterozygous mice (BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/+) did not show a pathological increase in body weight.
source: However, conditional Rai1 heterozygous mice (BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/+) did not show a pathological increase in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that non-BDNF-producing cells also contribute to SMS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: 26-week-old cKO male and female mice showed increased fat mass but not lean mass.
source: EcoMRI found that 26-week-old cKO male and female mice showed increased fat mass but not lean mass (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by EcoMRI data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Female cKO mice showed an increased mass of subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. Ing.) fat.
source: Further dissection of fat tissues from different organs showed an increased mass of subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. Ing.) fat in cKO mice of both sexes and an increased mass of epididymal adipose tissues (eWAT) in female cKOs (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by fat tissue measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Female cKO mice showed an increased mass of epididymal adipose tissues (eWAT).
source: Further dissection of fat tissues from different organs showed an increased mass of subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. Ing.) fat in cKO mice of both sexes and an increased mass of epididymal adipose tissues (eWAT) in female cKOs (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by fat tissue measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The total mass of brown adipose tissue (BAT) remained unchanged between groups.
source: In contrast, the total mass of brown adipose tissue (BAT) remained unchanged between groups (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by fat tissue measurements shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Both male and female cKO mice showed hypertrophic eWAT adipocytes.
source: In both male and female cKO mice, we found hypertrophic eWAT adipocytes (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4E) and elevated blood leptin levels (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is supported by histology data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Both male and female cKO mice showed elevated blood leptin levels.
source: In both male and female cKO mice, we found hypertrophic eWAT adipocytes (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4E) and elevated blood leptin levels (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is supported by blood leptin measurements shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: There was no significant alteration in blood lipids such as triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), low-density lipoproteins (LDL), and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in either male or female cKO mice.
source: However, there was no significant alteration in blood lipids such as triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), low-density lipoproteins (LDL), and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in either male or female cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by blood lipid measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4G–I.

claim: Male and female cKO mice did not have defects in respiratory exchange rates.
source: Similar to SMS mice, male and female cKO mice did not have defects in respiratory exchange rates when measured by indirect calorimetry (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4J).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4J.

claim: During the dark phase, female cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure.
source: During the dark phase, female cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure (Figure 2I) and decreased total locomotor activity (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Female cKO mice showed decreased total locomotor activity during the dark phase.
source: During the dark phase, female cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure (Figure 2I) and decreased total locomotor activity (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Total food intake remained unchanged in female cKO mice.
source: In contrast, total food intake remained unchanged (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Male cKO mice became hyperphagic.
source: Male cKO mice became hyperphagic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4K), showed increased energy expenditure during the dark phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 4L), and exhibited normal locomotor activity when compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4M).
evidence: This is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4K.

claim: Male cKO mice showed increased energy expenditure during the dark phase.
source: Male cKO mice became hyperphagic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4K), showed increased energy expenditure during the dark phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 4L), and exhibited normal locomotor activity when compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4M).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4L.

claim: Male cKO mice exhibited normal locomotor activity when compared to controls.
source: Male cKO mice became hyperphagic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4K), showed increased energy expenditure during the dark phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 4L), and exhibited normal locomotor activity when compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4M).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4M.

claim: cKO mice of both sexes showed normal blood glucose levels right before the glucose tolerance test but became hyperglycaemic 20 min (female cKO) and 45 min (male cKO) after glucose administration.
source: Interestingly, cKO mice of both sexes showed normal blood glucose levels right before the test but became hyperglycaemic 20 min (female cKO) and 45 min (male cKO) after glucose administration (Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 4N).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4N.

claim: cKO mice showed a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) for blood glucose levels during the glucose tolerance test.
source: This change was accompanied by a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) for both groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 3I, Figure 2—figure supplement 4O).
evidence: This is supported by AUC calculations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4O.

claim: Increased blood insulin levels were found during the GTT in both sexes of cKO mice.
source: We also found increased blood insulin levels during the GTT in both sexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J, Figure 2—figure supplement 4P).
evidence: This is supported by insulin measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4P.

claim: Female cKO mice showed moderately elevated glucose levels 20 min into the insulin tolerance test.
source: In the insulin tolerance test (ITT), female cKO mice showed moderately elevated glucose levels 20 min into the test (Figure 2—figure supplement 3K).
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3K.

claim: Male cKO mice showed considerably higher glucose levels than controls in the ITT during the 60–120 min intervals.
source: By contrast, male cKO mice showed considerably higher glucose levels than controls in the ITT (~6.5 ng/ml for cKO and ~2.0 ng/ml for Ctrl) during the 60–120 min intervals (Figure 2—figure supplement 4Q).
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4Q.

claim: A hyperpolarized step followed by increasing the holding voltage at resting membrane potentials (Rm) was able to initiate rebound firing or rebound repetitive firing in most PVHBDNF neurons.
source: We found that a hyperpolarized step followed by increasing the holding voltage at resting membrane potentials (Rm) was able to initiate rebound firing or rebound repetitive firing in most PVHBDNF neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed reduced action potential (AP) firing frequency at a holding voltage of –60 mV compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons.
source: cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed reduced action potential (AP) firing frequency at a holding voltage of –60 mV compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The resting membrane potential (Rm) of cKO neurons showed a 10 mV positive shift compared to Ctrl neurons.
source: The resting membrane potential (Rm) of cKO (–52 mV) neurons showed a 10 mV positive shift compared to Ctrl neurons (–62 mV) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fewer cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed spontaneous firing at Rm compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons.
source: We also found that fewer cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed spontaneous firing at Rm (Figure 3E, Ctrl:10/13; cKO:5/12) and at a holding voltage of –70 mV (Figure 3F, Ctrl:6/12; cKO:1/12) compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Fewer cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed spontaneous firing at a holding voltage of –70 mV compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons.
source: We also found that fewer cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed spontaneous firing at Rm (Figure 3E, Ctrl:10/13; cKO:5/12) and at a holding voltage of –70 mV (Figure 3F, Ctrl:6/12; cKO:1/12) compared to Ctrl PVHBDNF neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The threshold of the first AP initiated by a ramp current injection (1 nA/s) from Rm was significantly increased in cKO neurons.
source: The threshold of the first AP initiated by a ramp current injection (1 nA/s) from Rm was significantly increased in cKO neurons (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a lower peak amplitude (measuring from the threshold to peak).
source: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a lower peak amplitude (measuring from the threshold to peak) (Figure 3I), a normal threshold (Figure 3J), and a normal half-width (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a normal threshold.
source: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a lower peak amplitude (measuring from the threshold to peak) (Figure 3I), a normal threshold (Figure 3J), and a normal half-width (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a normal half-width.
source: The AP of the cKO group exhibited a lower peak amplitude (measuring from the threshold to peak) (Figure 3I), a normal threshold (Figure 3J), and a normal half-width (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: cKO PVHBDNF neurons showed a significantly increased AUC for mIPSC.
source: However, we observed a significantly increased AUC (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3M.

claim: cKO PVHBDNF neurons had a smaller cellular diameter.
source: Interestingly, we found that cKO PVHBDNF neurons had a smaller cellular diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Bilateral administration of two adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) into the PVH of female BdnfCre/+ mice at 3 wk of age resulted in a significant loss of Rai1 protein expression in PVHBDNF neurons.
source: Bilateral administration of two adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) into the PVH of female BdnfCre/+ mice (Exp group) at 3 wk of age resulted in a significant loss of Rai1 protein expression in PVHBDNF neurons when compared to BdnfCre/+ mice injected with an AAV encoding the sgRai1 and GFP (Ctrl group) (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The total number of BDNF+ cells were not different in the Ctrl and Exp groups.
source: Quantification of AAV-infected (GFP+) BDNF neurons showed that while the total number of BDNF+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and BDNF+ GFP+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) cells were not different in the two groups, the percentage of AAV-infected BDNF+ cells that express RAI1 was significantly reduced in the Exp group (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The total number of BDNF+ GFP+ cells were not different in the Ctrl and Exp groups.
source: Quantification of AAV-infected (GFP+) BDNF neurons showed that while the total number of BDNF+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and BDNF+ GFP+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) cells were not different in the two groups, the percentage of AAV-infected BDNF+ cells that express RAI1 was significantly reduced in the Exp group (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The percentage of AAV-infected BDNF+ cells that express RAI1 was significantly reduced in the Exp group.
source: Quantification of AAV-infected (GFP+) BDNF neurons showed that while the total number of BDNF+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and BDNF+ GFP+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) cells were not different in the two groups, the percentage of AAV-infected BDNF+ cells that express RAI1 was significantly reduced in the Exp group (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The virus expression did not spread to the non-PVH neighbouring nuclei.
source: Moreover, the virus expression did not spread to the non-PVH neighbouring nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Deleting Rai1 from the PVHBDNF neurons resulted in a significant increase in body weight beginning at 17 wk of age.
source: Deleting Rai1 from the PVHBDNF neurons resulted in a significant increase in body weight beginning at 17 wk of age (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Obesity in 26-week-old Exp mice was due to increased fat mass.
source: Similar to the cKO (BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/fl) mice, obesity in 26-week-old Exp mice was due to increased fat mass (Figure 4E) and more specifically, increased subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. ing) and epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) but not BAT (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by EcoMRI data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Exp mice showed increased subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. ing) and epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) but not BAT.
source: Similar to the cKO (BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/fl) mice, obesity in 26-week-old Exp mice was due to increased fat mass (Figure 4E) and more specifically, increased subcutaneous inguinal (S.C. ing) and epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) but not BAT (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by fat tissue measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: eWAT adipocytes became hypertrophic in Exp mice.
source: We also found that eWAT adipocytes became hypertrophic (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by histology data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Food intake did not differ between Exp and Ctrl groups.
source: Similar to the cKO mice, food intake did not differ between Exp and Ctrl groups (Figure 4H), likely due to the high level of satiety signals in the brain caused by increased blood leptin levels (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Exp mice showed increased blood leptin levels.
source: Similar to the cKO mice, food intake did not differ between Exp and Ctrl groups (Figure 4H), likely due to the high level of satiety signals in the brain caused by increased blood leptin levels (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by blood leptin measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Energy expenditure was similar in Exp and Ctrl groups.
source: We also found that energy expenditure (Figure 4J), respiratory exchange rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), and blood lipid parameters, including TG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), HDL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), LDL and VLDL levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), were similar in Exp and Ctrl groups, consistent with the cKO data (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Respiratory exchange rate was similar in Exp and Ctrl groups.
source: We also found that energy expenditure (Figure 4J), respiratory exchange rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), and blood lipid parameters, including TG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), HDL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), LDL and VLDL levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), were similar in Exp and Ctrl groups, consistent with the cKO data (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Blood lipid parameters, including TG, HDL, LDL and VLDL levels, were similar in Exp and Ctrl groups.
source: We also found that energy expenditure (Figure 4J), respiratory exchange rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), and blood lipid parameters, including TG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), HDL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), LDL and VLDL levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), were similar in Exp and Ctrl groups, consistent with the cKO data (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by blood lipid measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, 1I, and 1J.

claim: Exp mice showed significantly less locomotor activity during the dark phase than the Ctrl mice.
source: Interestingly, Exp mice showed significantly less locomotor activity during the dark phase than the Ctrl mice (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Exp mice have a hyperglycaemic profile in the glucose tolerance test.
source: A GTT indicated that Exp mice have a hyperglycaemic profile (Figure 4L), accompanied by a slightly higher AUC for blood glucose levels (p=0.05) (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Exp mice showed a slightly higher AUC for blood glucose levels during the glucose tolerance test (p=0.05).
source: A GTT indicated that Exp mice have a hyperglycaemic profile (Figure 4L), accompanied by a slightly higher AUC for blood glucose levels (p=0.05) (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is supported by AUC calculations shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Insulin levels in Exp mice were significantly elevated 15 min after glucose administration.
source: Insulin levels in Exp mice were also significantly elevated 15 min after glucose administration (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by insulin measurements shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Saline-treated SMS mice showed reduced phosphorylated-AKT (p-AKT) levels in the hypothalamus.
source: Consistent with the reduced neurotrophin signalling observed in our proteomic analysis, saline-treated SMS mice showed reduced phosphorylated-AKT (p-AKT; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1) levels in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment significantly increased the levels of p-AKT in the SMS mice 1 hr post-treatment.
source: LM22A-4 treatment significantly increased the levels of p-AKT in the SMS mice 1 hr post-treatment (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1), indicating increased signalling downstream of the BDNF pathway.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Saline-treated SMS mice were significantly heavier than saline-treated control mice from 9 wk of age onwards.
source: Saline-treated SMS mice (Figure 5C) were significantly heavier than saline-treated control mice from 9 wk of age onwards.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LM22A-4-treated SMS mice showed a similar body weight to saline-treated control littermates until 13 wk of age but became obese by 14 wk of age.
source: Interestingly, LM22A-4-treated SMS mice showed a similar body weight to saline-treated control littermates until 13 wk of age but became obese by 14 wk of age (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LM22A-4-treated SMS mice were significantly less obese than saline-treated SMS mice throughout the treatment period.
source: Consistent with a partial rescue, LM22A-4-treated SMS mice were significantly less obese than saline-treated SMS mice throughout the treatment period (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Control mice treated with LM22A-4 did not show a further reduction in body weight.
source: Control mice treated with LM22A-4 did not show a further reduction in body weight (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the therapeutic effects were specific to SMS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LM22A-4 did not significantly rescue increased food intake in SMS mice.
source: We measured food intake and found that LM22A-4 did not significantly rescue increased food intake in SMS mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SMS mice showed normal energy expenditure.
source: SMS mice showed normal energy expenditure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and respiratory exchange rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), neither of which was altered by LM22A-4 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SMS mice showed normal respiratory exchange rate.
source: SMS mice showed normal energy expenditure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and respiratory exchange rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), neither of which was altered by LM22A-4 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued locomotor activity in SMS mice.
source: Interestingly, we did observe a partial rescue of locomotor activity in LM22A-4-treated SMS mice that was not significantly different from saline-treated Ctrl or SMS mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued fat deposition in SMS mice.
source: We also found that the LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued fat deposition (Figure 5H) and completely rescued HDL levels (Figure 5I) in SMS mice.
evidence: This is supported by fat tissue measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment completely rescued HDL levels in SMS mice.
source: We also found that the LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued fat deposition (Figure 5H) and completely rescued HDL levels (Figure 5I) in SMS mice.
evidence: This is supported by blood lipid measurements shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Saline-treated SMS mice showed increased baseline insulin levels during an ITT.
source: During an ITT, we found that saline-treated SMS mice showed increased baseline insulin levels (Figure 5J) and blood glucose levels during the test (Figure 5K), both of which were partially rescued by LM22A-4 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by insulin measurements shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Saline-treated SMS mice showed increased blood glucose levels during the insulin tolerance test.
source: During an ITT, we found that saline-treated SMS mice showed increased baseline insulin levels (Figure 5J) and blood glucose levels during the test (Figure 5K), both of which were partially rescued by LM22A-4 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment partially rescued increased baseline insulin levels and blood glucose levels during the insulin tolerance test in SMS mice.
source: During an ITT, we found that saline-treated SMS mice showed increased baseline insulin levels (Figure 5J) and blood glucose levels during the test (Figure 5K), both of which were partially rescued by LM22A-4 treatment.
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 5J and 5K.

claim: Saline-treated SMS mice showed significantly more rearing behaviour when compared to the saline-treated controls.
source: Saline-treated SMS mice showed significantly more rearing behaviour when compared to the saline-treated controls (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment reduced the repetitive rearing behaviour in SMS mice.
source: Interestingly, the LM22A-4 treatment reduced the repetitive rearing behaviour in SMS mice (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment did not change repetitive behaviours in control mice.
source: LM22A-4 treatment did not change repetitive behaviours in control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), suggesting the effect is specific to Rai1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: LM22A-4 treatment did not rescue social dominance deficits in SMS mice.
source: However, we did not observe a rescue of social dominance deficits in SMS mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by tube test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: RAI1 is enriched in BDNF-producing neurons in the mouse PVH.
source: Specifically, 55% of PVHBDNF neurons express RAI1, whereas only 2% of PVHOxytocin neurons express RAI1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I). These data suggest that RAI1 is enriched in BDNF-producing neurons in the mouse PVH.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression pattern of RAI1 in PVHBDNF neurons versus PVHOxytocin neurons.

claim: Non-BDNF-producing cells also contribute to SMS pathogenesis.
source: However, conditional Rai1 heterozygous mice (BdnfCre/+; Rai1fl/+) did not show a pathological increase in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that non-BDNF-producing cells also contribute to SMS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heterozygous deletion of Rai1 in BDNF-producing cells is not sufficient to induce obesity, while SMS mice (with global Rai1 haploinsufficiency) do show obesity.

claim: Obesity in male cKO mice is attributable to overeating despite increased energy expenditure.
source: Male cKO mice became hyperphagic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4K), showed increased energy expenditure during the dark phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 4L), and exhibited normal locomotor activity when compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4M). These results suggest that obesity in male cKO mice is attributable to overeating despite increased energy expenditure.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of increased food intake and increased energy expenditure in male cKO mice.

claim: Reduced PVHBDNF neuronal activity upon Rai1 loss could potentially explain obesity.
source: Reduced PVHBDNF neuronal activity upon Rai1 loss could potentially explain obesity, consistent with a previous report that found chemogenetic activation of PVHBDNF neurons promotes negative energy balance by decreasing feeding and increasing energy expenditure (Wu and Xu, 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced neuronal activity in cKO PVHBDNF neurons and the known role of PVHBDNF neurons in energy balance.

claim: RAI1 regulates body weight and metabolic function through hypothalamic BDNF-producing neurons.
source: These data argue that RAI1 regulates body weight and metabolic function through hypothalamic BDNF-producing neurons and that targeting neurotrophin downstream signalling might improve associated SMS phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Targeting neurotrophin downstream signalling might improve associated SMS phenotypes.
source: These data argue that RAI1 regulates body weight and metabolic function through hypothalamic BDNF-producing neurons and that targeting neurotrophin downstream signalling might improve associated SMS phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the LM22A-4 treatment experiments.

claim: Dysfunction of BDNF-producing cells could contribute to SMS pathogenesis.
source: Together, these results suggest that Rai1 loss impairs specific pathways, including neurotrophin signalling, and indicate that dysfunction of BDNF-producing cells could contribute to SMS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neurotrophin signalling is disrupted in SMS mice and that Rai1 deletion from BDNF-producing cells induces obesity.

claim: BDNF-producing cells depend on RAI1 to regulate body weight homeostasis.
source: These experiments demonstrate that BDNF-producing cells depend on RAI1 to regulate body weight, adiposity, glucose, and insulin tolerance in mice.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the results section and supported by the cKO experiments.

claim: PVHBDNF neurons depend on RAI1 to regulate energy homeostasis.
source: Conditional deletion of Rai1 from PVHBDNF neurons during adolescence impairs the regulation of body weight, adiposity, glucose tolerance, and locomotion. These changes recapitulate most phenotypes observed in cKO mice with Rai1 deleted in BDNF-producing cells from early development.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the results section and supported by the AAV-mediated Rai1 deletion experiments.

claim: Dysfunction of BDNF downstream signalling contributes to obesity associated with SMS mice.
source: Our work indicates that PVHBDNF neurons depend on RAI1 to maintain normal neuronal activity and regulate body weight homeostasis, and dysfunction of BDNF downstream signalling contributes to obesity associated with SMS mice.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction and supported by the LM22A-4 treatment experiments.

claim: Enhancing BDNF-TRKB signalling should be explored as a future therapeutic avenue for obesity and metabolic conditions associated with reduced neurotrophin signalling.
source: Nevertheless, our work identifies RAI1 as a novel regulator of the neuronal excitability of PVHBDNF neurons. This regulation is critical for regulating food intake and energy expenditure. Our evidence suggests that BDNF-producing neurons are involved in SMS pathogenesis and that enhancing BDNF-TRKB signalling should be explored as a future therapeutic avenue for obesity and metabolic conditions associated with reduced neurotrophin signalling (Xu and Xie, 2016).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by the LM22A-4 treatment experiments.
